units.title: 1. Blood Supply of the Brain and the Circle of Willis
units.sec: Carotid Terminal Branches and Circle of Willis
units.guide:
The anterior circulation figure traces the brachiocephalic trunk to the right common carotid and the right internal carotid artery, with the basilar, vertebral, subclavian and posterior communicating arteries and the C1-C6 levels all labelled, and gives the terminal branches of the internal carotid artery under the mnemonic OPAAm.
Those branches are the ophthalmic artery, posterior communicating artery, anterior choroidal artery, anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery.
The circle-of-Willis diagram then names the A1 and A2 segments of the ACA around the anterior communicating artery, the MCA, anterior choroidal and posterior communicating arteries at the ICA, and the P1 and P2 segments of the posterior cerebral artery on the basilar artery with its superior cerebellar, pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar and posterior inferior cerebellar branches, the vertebral arteries and the anterior spinal artery.

units.title: 2. Blood Supply of the Surface of the Brain
units.guide:
The three colour-coded brain diagrams shade the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral artery territories over the superolateral, medial and inferior surfaces.
In the ACA-MCA-PCA table the ACA supplies most of the medial surface with the paracentral lobule, cingulate gyrus and a narrow strip of cortex along the superomedial border; the MCA supplies most of the superolateral surface including most of the primary motor and sensory areas, the frontal eye field, Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the dominant hemisphere and the temporal pole; the PCA supplies most of the inferior surface except the temporal pole.

units.title: 3. ACA, MCA and PCA Injury Features
units.sec: Injury Syndromes of the Three Arteries
units.guide:
ACA injury gives weakness that is LL greater than UL, urinary incontinence from paracentral lobule involvement, and the cingulate gyrus picture of apathy as the mild form, abulia, amotivation and akinetic mutism as the severe form.
MCA injury gives UL greater than LL weakness, temporal-pole involvement with macular involvement, and a cortical aphasia pairing Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus with Wernicke's area in the superior temporal gyrus, in contrast to internal capsule lesions where there is no aphasia.
PCA injury produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing from visual-area damage.

units.title: 4. Parts of the Internal Capsule and Their Fibre Content
units.guide:
The internal capsule is drawn between the caudate head, lentiform nucleus and thalamus, with the genu carrying the corticobulbar tract, the anterior limb the anterior thalamic radiation and frontopontine and other corticofugal fibres, and the posterior limb the corticospinal tract with superior thalamic, auditory and optic radiations around the medial and lateral geniculate nuclei; the corona radiata, caudate, putamen, globus pallidus and thalamus are labelled on the coronal section.
The parts list assigns frontopontine fibres with lacunar strokes and cerebellar involvement to the anterior limb, corticospinal fibres for head and neck with predominant corticobulbar fibres to the genu, the corticospinal tract in the anterior two-thirds of the posterior limb with UL equal to LL weakness and corticorubral fibres, the posterior thalamic optic radiation to the retrolentiform part and the inferior thalamic auditory radiation to the sublentiform part.

units.title: 5. Corticobulbar Injury Patterns, Capsular Notes and the HHH Triad
units.sec: Corticobulbar Patterns and the HHH Triad
units.guide:
Unilateral corticobulbar injury produces no cranial nerve palsy because of bilateral cortical innervation, except a contralateral upper-motor-neuron seventh palsy due to its contralateral supply, while bilateral corticobulbar injury gives pseudobulbar palsy as seen in ALS or motor neuron disease; a dense capsular lesion causes contralateral facial palsy with hemiplegia.
An internal capsule lesion is printed as the HHH triad of hemiplegia that is dense with UL equal to LL and a contralateral UMN seventh palsy, hemisensory loss, and homonymous hemianopia, and the closing note separates MCA involvement with UL greater than LL, ACA involvement with LL greater than UL, and posterior-limb weakness with UL equal to LL.

units.title: 6. Arterial Supply of the Internal Capsule
units.guide:
The upper diagram lists four supply lines: striate branches of the middle cerebral artery, the recurrent branch of the anterior cerebral artery, branches from the internal carotid and posterior communicating arteries, and the anterior choroidal artery, with the annotation that retrolentiform injury gives a mild HHH triad in which hemisensory loss predominates.
The boxed anterior limb is supplied by anterior cerebral striate branches, including the longest branch, the recurrent artery of Heubner, together with middle cerebral branches; the genu receives anterior and middle cerebral striate branches plus direct internal carotid branches.
The posterior limb is supplied by middle cerebral striate branches including the large Charcot artery of cerebral haemorrhage and by the anterior choroidal artery, while the sublentiform part takes posterior cerebral and anterior choroidal branches and the retrolentiform part takes posterior cerebral branches only.

units.title: 7. MCA Segments, Sylvian Divisions and Lenticulostriate Occlusion
units.guide:
The MCA figure labels the horizontal M1, sylvian M2 and cortical M3 segments with the medial and lateral lenticulo-striate arteries against the putamen, globus pallidus, internal capsule and caudate head.
The M2 annotation supplies the sylvian fissure and splits into a superior division whose stroke causes contralateral hemiplegia with Broca's aphasia and an inferior division whose stroke causes Wernicke's aphasia without weakness, while both divisions together give contralateral hemiplegia with global aphasia.
The M1 segment supplies the internal capsule, caudate nucleus, putamen and globus pallidus through lenticulostriate arteries and 30-300 micrometre perforators; occlusion gives internal capsule stroke with the HHH triad plus a UMN seventh palsy and parkinsonian features when bilateral, and lipohyalinosis of the perforators gives lacunar stroke with pure motor hemiparesis.

units.title: 8. Complete MCA Syndrome versus Capsular Lesions, and the ACA Segments
units.sec: Complete MCA Syndrome and the ACA
units.guide:
Complete MCA syndrome follows involvement of the M1, M2 and M3 segments, giving aphasia with a seventh nerve palsy only if corticobulbar involvement is bilateral, plus the HHH triad; the comparison table keeps the HHH triad as the common feature but separates the cortical syndrome by aphasia, agnosia, apraxia, loss of consciousness and seizures, with non-dominant unstructured dressing apraxia and hemispatial neglect, against the dense hemiplegia with UL equal to LL of a capsular lesion.
The ACA splits at the anterior communicating artery: the A1 segment proximal to it supplies the anterior hypothalamus, caudate lobe and anterior limb of the internal capsule and, because of significant collaterals, its occlusion produces no clinical symptoms, while the A2 segment distal to it supplies the medial cerebral surface with contralateral hemiplegia worse in the leg, the paracentral lobule with urinary incontinence and the cingulate gyrus with apathy and abulia.

units.title: 9. PCA Segments, Unilateral and Bilateral Involvement
units.guide:
The PCA is divided at the posterior communicating artery into a P1 segment supplying the midbrain, subthalamus and thalamus, and a P2 segment whose unilateral involvement produces the medial-temporal picture of visual agnosia, peduncular hallucinosis, alexia without agraphia from splenium involvement and memory disturbance from the hippocampus, and occipital involvement giving congruent contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
Bilateral P2 involvement produces Anton syndrome of cortical blindness with pupillary sparing and Balint syndrome of optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia, simultanagnosia and palinopsia, and a note separates ataxia with agraphia as Gerstmann syndrome.

units.title: 10. Types of Posterior Circulation, Artery of Percheron and Dejerine-Roussy Syndrome
units.guide:
Four schematic types of posterior circulation are drawn, each labelling the midbrain, both thalami, the posterior cerebral artery and the basilar artery, with type IIB showing the artery of Percheron.
Infarction of that single thalamic perforator is printed as a triad of drowsiness or confusion, vertical gaze palsy and memory disturbance.
Dejerine-Roussy syndrome, the burning hand syndrome from thalamogeniculate artery occlusion, produces contralateral hemisensory loss with burning pain in the upper and lower limb, illustrated by the axial MRI captioned for that syndrome.

units.title: 11. Watershed Territories and Their Predisposing Conditions
units.guide:
The watershed panel of axial FLAIR and diffusion images is set against a schematic that labels the cortical border zone between the ACA and MCA, the internal border zone between the lenticulostriate circulation, printed as LCA, and the MCA, and the cortical border zone between the MCA and PCA.
Watershed areas are stated to be prone to infarct, with predisposing conditions of hypoalbuminaemia, sudden hypotension and dehydration, alongside the printed reminder to maintain adequate hydration of the patient.
